clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says making money has never been easier.

Growing up, every rich person in his town owned a business, and the only way in was years of apprenticeship with no guarantee of a payoff. Today you can learn how to do a heart transplant free on YouTube.

He's seen the proof: guys starting with under $100, and two brothers he knows who went from zero to a $65 million mansion in Beverly Hills, built entirely online.

clips.send: A guy with a business idea sends this to his cousin chasing ten side hustles at once - the contrarian truth that Henry Ford didn't invent anything, he just focused and copied better, and anger at every shiny object that wasted their time.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says most people fail in business because they can't pick a lane.

He calls it riding two horses to the finish line - chasing every opportunity instead of committing to one, what Napoleon Hill called singleness of purpose.

Once you've picked your lane: find a need and fill it, or build a better mousetrap. Henry Ford didn't invent the car - people already had horses. He just built a better way to get around, and it made him one of the richest men alive.

clips.send: A friend forwards this to someone who's been 'thinking about it' for six months - the uncomfortable reminder that waiting is still a decision, and the anxiety that stalling is quietly costing them money.
clips.caption:
J. Paul Getty was once the richest man alive, and he said the habit that separates rich from poor isn't talent - it's decisiveness.

Successful people live by success habits without even realizing it. Jim Rohn put it this way: character is following through on a decision long after the excitement has worn off.

Here's the part people miss - deciding to wait is still a decision. What you can't do is drift with no decision at all.

clips.send: A guy grinding through a boring job sends this to a friend who says they have no motivation - the wild fact that Michael Jordan made up fake rivalries in his head to win six championships, awe that anyone can steal the same trick for free.
clips.caption:
Michael Jordan admitted something wild in The Last Dance - a lot of his motivation wasn't even real.

Kevin Trudeau explains the trick: Jordan would convince himself someone disrespected him, even when it never happened, just so he had a reason to destroy them on the court. Tom Brady did the same thing chasing ring after ring.

It's called creating a game in your mind, and it works in any job - there's even a book called The Game of Work about it.

What game could you invent to get through tomorrow?

#kevintrudeau #michaeljordan #mindset #motivation #thelastdance #mentalgame

clips.send: A real estate agent panicking about the market sends this to a colleague ready to quit - the true story of two Detroit realtors in the same recession, one going bankrupt and one getting rich on mindset alone, awe mixed with a jolt of anxiety about which one they're being.
clips.caption:
Zig Ziglar told this story about a strike at Detroit's Big Three automakers, and Kevin Trudeau calls it the best proof of mindset he's ever heard.

One real estate agent panicked - 85% of the town wasn't working, and he said another six weeks of the strike would bankrupt him.

The woman next to him, same city, same business, was thriving - laid-off couples finally had time to shop for their dream home, and she hoped the strike lasted so she'd get rich.

Same recession, same product, same customers. One went bankrupt. One got rich.

Which one are you being right now?

#kevintrudeau #zigziglar #mindset #recession #realestate #successmindset

clips.send: A guy setting a $50K goal for next year sends this to himself as a reset - the trick that dreaming in trillions makes six figures feel like nothing, awe at the size of the dream mixed with hope that it actually works.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says he's sat in rooms with people running trillion-dollar hedge funds and sovereign wealth funds like Norway's - and it changed how he sets goals.

The trick: dream absurdly big first - $100 million, even a billion - then come back to reality and set your real goal, like $100,000 a year. Suddenly it feels easy, almost like a joke.

He compares it to coach Dick Vermeel, who drilled his players so hard that game day felt like a cakewalk.

Stretch your mind first. Everything smaller becomes simple.
